articles.title: The effect of pregnancy and puerperium on haemorrhage risk in women with cerebral cavernous malformations: a case-crossover study.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) are lesions that may be incidental or present with haemorrhage or focal neurological deficits. Some authors have reported apparent lesion enlargement during pregnancy and hypothesised that hormonal fluctuations may promote CCM growth or haemorrhage. Whether pregnancy increases the risk of symptomatic haemorrhage (SH) from CCMs therefore represents an important clinical concern.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: We collected prospective data from patients with CCMs. A case-crossover framework was used to compare the risk of SH during pregnancy-related and non-pregnant observation periods. Pregnancy-related observation periods included pregnancy and the 6-week puerperium, while all other follow-up time after CCM diagnosis was considered non-pregnant. Each woman served as her own control, with the risk of SH during pregnancy-related periods compared with that during her non-pregnant follow-up periods.
RESULTS: After screening, the final cohort included 42 women diagnosed with a CCM at 46 years of age or younger. Of these, 23 women experienced at least 1 pregnancy (30.4% familial CCM; 21.7% brainstem CCM) at or after CCM diagnosis, accounting for 40 pregnancies. Overall, 2 SHs occurred during 25.6 pregnancy patient-years, corresponding to an annual SH rate of 7.8% (95% CI, 0.9-28.3), compared with 42 SHs during 420.7 non-pregnancy patient-years, corresponding to an annual SH rate of 10.0% (95% CI, 7.2-13.5). No statistically significant difference was found in the haemorrhagic rates between pregnant vs non-pregnant periods (P = .751). When observation periods were stratified according to a history of prior haemorrhage, no SHs occurred during 10.3 pregnancy patient-years among periods with prior haemorrhage, whereas 8 SHs occurred during 12.7 non-pregnancy patient-years, corresponding to an annual SH rate of 63.0% (95% CI, 27.2-124.2). Among periods without prior haemorrhage, 2 SHs occurred during 15.2 pregnancy patient-years, corresponding to an annual SH rate of 13.1% (95% CI, 1.6-47.5), compared with 34 SHs during 408.0 non-pregnancy patient-years, corresponding to an annual SH rate of 8.3% (95% CI, 5.8-11.6). In this subgroup, generalised estimating equation (GEE)-Poisson analysis showed no significant difference in haemorrhage risk between pregnancy and non-pregnancy periods (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 1.64, 95% CI, 0.44-6.13; P = .462). When analysis was restricted to brainstem CCMs, GEE-Poisson analysis showed no significant difference between pregnancy and non-pregnancy periods (IRR 2.09; 95% CI, 0.36-12.14; P = .411). One SH occurred during 8.2 pregnancy patient-years, corresponding to an annual SH rate of 12.2% (95% CI, 0.3-67.9), vs 6 SHs during 91.6 non-pregnancy patient-years, corresponding to 6.6% (95% CI, 2.4-14.3). Among periods with prior haemorrhage, no SHs occurred during 1.5 pregnancy patient-years (0.0%; 95% CI, 0.0-194.7), vs 2 SHs during 4.4 non-pregnancy patient-years (45.2%; 95% CI, 5.5-163.4). Among periods without prior haemorrhage, 1 SH occurred during 6.7 pregnancy patient-years (15.0%; 95% CI, 0.4-83.6), vs 4 SHs during 87.2 non-pregnancy patient-years (4.6%; 95% CI, 1.3-11.7), with no significant difference on GEE-Poisson analysis (IRR 3.50; 95% CI, 0.62-19.78; P = .156).
CONCLUSION: Pregnancy was not associated with a significantly increased rate of SH in this cohort of women with CCMs. However, the limited number of events during pregnancy and the limited pregnant follow-up require cautious interpretation. Counselling should remain individualised according to lesion location, prior haemorrhagic history, neurological status and treatment history.

articles.title: When a Seizure Reveals More Than a Hemorrhage: When to Suspect Cerebral Cavernous Malformations.
articles.abstract: Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) are low-flow vascular malformations that may be asymptomatic or present with seizures, hemorrhage, headache, or focal neurological deficits. Most are sporadic and solitary, whereas familial CCMs are associated with multiple lesions and autosomal-dominant inheritance. Distinguishing between these forms is clinically relevant for long-term management. We present a 33-year-old woman who presented with generalized tonic-clonic seizures following sleep deprivation. Computed tomography (CT) initially suggested a left frontal intraparenchymal hemorrhage. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) subsequently revealed two left frontal Zabramski type II CCMs. Electroencephalography showed cortical dysfunction with paroxysmal activity and contralateral propagation. Antiseizure treatment with phenytoin was initiated and later supplemented with levetiracetam. The patient remained asymptomatic and was referred for tertiary evaluation. This case highlights the diagnostic limitations of CT and the importance of MRI for CCM characterization and detection of multiple lesions. The presence of two cavernomas and a potentially relevant family history raises suspicion for familial CCM, although these findings alone do not establish a hereditary diagnosis. Genetic evaluation and detailed family assessment should therefore be considered. Treatment should be individualized; conservative management is appropriate in selected stable patients, whereas microsurgery and stereotactic radiosurgery are reserved for specific clinical scenarios.

articles.title: Head-Mounted Augmented Reality in the Planning of Cerebral Cavernous Malformation Resections: Demonstrating Feasibility Through an Initial Case Series.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Lesion localization, associated vascular structures, and corticotomy selection pose key challenges when planning cerebral cavernous malformation (CCM) resections in eloquent areas. Head-mounted augmented reality (HMAR) may improve visualization without the gaze disruptions imposed by conventional neuronavigation. This study investigated the preoperative feasibility of HMAR in surgical plan modifications and educational value.
METHODS: We performed a single-center retrospective review of all CCM patients with HMAR-assisted preoperative planning from 1 September, 2022, to 31 August, 2024. Three-dimensional reconstructions of patients' magnetic resonance imaging were viewed preoperatively using HMAR. Registration accuracy was confirmed against conventional neuronavigation. Surgical plan modifications entailed alterations of the operative goal, trajectory, or steps. Educational value of HMAR was appraised by trainees as "not helpful" when only confirming existing plans, "helpful" when facilitating a greater understanding of the lesion, and "very helpful" when spurring additional positioning or plan modifications.
RESULTS: Of 19 patients with CCM resections, 14 patients with HMAR-assisted preoperative planning were included. The average age was 38.6 ± 14.5 years, with 6 males and 8 females. Three of 14 (21%) surgical approaches were modified following HMAR use: two to minimize cortical disruption and one to avoid injuring an associated developmental venous anomaly. Registration was accurate in all cases. Between registration and utilization, HMAR added an average of 2.7 ± 1.0 min in the operating room. The mean appraisal of the educational value of HMAR was "helpful."
CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative planning with HMAR prompted surgical plan modifications and often improved trainees' understanding without introducing significant workflow disruptions. Three-dimensional visualization offered dynamic spatial details beyond traditional two-dimensional multiplanar MRI.

articles.title: ESR Essentials: susceptibility-weighted imaging-practice recommendations by the European Society for Magnetic Resonance in Medicine and Biology.
articles.abstract: Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) is a high-resolution 3D gradient-echo (GRE) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technique that combines magnitude and phase information to increase sensitivity to blood products, iron, calcification, thrombus, and venous structures. In routine practice, SWI should be interpreted together with source magnitude images, filtered phase images, processed SWI images, and minimum-intensity projection (minIP) images, keeping in mind blooming and other artefacts, as well as vendor-dependent phase conventions. Its most established role is in brain MRI, particularly in: suspected cerebral amyloid angiopathy; baseline and follow-up assessment of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with haemosiderin deposition (ARIA-H) during anti-amyloid therapy; traumatic brain injury; multiple sclerosis work-up, when assessment of the central vein sign or paramagnetic rim lesions is clinically relevant; neuro-oncology; and vascular malformations. Overall, these constitute the core recommended brain scenarios for SWI supported by moderate to high levels of evidence. Outside neuroradiology (e.g., musculoskeletal, abdominal, breast, pelvic, and cardiac imaging), SWI remains promising but less standardised and should currently be reserved for selected problem-solving indications. KEY POINTS: SWI should be acquired as a high-resolution 3D GRE sequence and interpreted together with source magnitude images, filtered phase images, and post-processed minIP images, keeping in mind blooming and other artefacts, as well as vendor-specific phase conventions. SWI should be included in brain MRI protocols when haemorrhagic or microvascular susceptibility findings are expected to affect diagnosis or management, especially in cerebral amyloid angiopathy, anti-amyloid therapy monitoring, traumatic brain injury, and neuro-oncology or multiple sclerosis work-up. Outside neuroradiology, SWI can be used as a targeted problem-solving adjunct rather than as a routine sequence.

articles.title: Evaluation and management of neck masses in children.
articles.abstract: Neck masses in children usually fall into one of three categories: developmental, inflammatory/reactive, or neoplastic. Common congenital developmental masses in the neck include thyroglossal duct cysts, branchial cleft cysts, dermoid cysts, vascular malformations, and hemangiomas. Inflammatory neck masses can be the result of reactive lymphadenopathy, infectious lymphadenitis (viral, staphylococcal, and mycobacterial infections; cat-scratch disease), or Kawasaki disease. Common benign neoplastic lesions include pilomatrixomas, lipomas, fibromas, neurofibromas, and salivary gland tumors. Although rare in children, malignant lesions occurring in the neck include lymphoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, thyroid carcinoma, and metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Workup for a neck mass may include a complete blood count; purified protein derivative test for tuberculosis; and measurement of titers for Epstein-Barr virus, cat-scratch disease, cytomegalovirus, human immunodeficiency virus, and toxoplasmosis if the history raises suspicion for any of these conditions. Ultrasonography is the preferred imaging study for a developmental or palpable mass. Computed tomography with intravenous contrast media is recommended for evaluating a malignancy or a suspected retropharyngeal or deep neck abscess. Congenital neck masses are excised to prevent potential growth and secondary infection of the lesion. Antibiotic therapy for suspected bacterial lymphadenitis should target Staphylococcus aureus and group A streptococcus. Lack of response to initial antibiotics should prompt consideration of intravenous antibiotic therapy, referral for possible incision and drainage, or further workup. If malignancy is suspected (accompanying type B symptoms; hard, firm, or rubbery consistency; fixed mass; supraclavicular mass; lymph node larger than 2 cm in diameter; persistent enlargement for more than two weeks; no decrease in size after four to six weeks; absence of inflammation; ulceration; failure to respond to antibiotic therapy; or a thyroid mass), the patient should be referred to a head and neck surgeon for urgent evaluation and possible biopsy.

articles.title: Management of bleeding uterine arteriovenous malformation with bilateral uterine artery embolization.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate the technical feasibility and clinical outcome of bilateral uterine artery embolization (UAE) as a first-line therapeutic option for bleeding uterine arteriovenous malformation (AVM).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Between 2002 and 2012, 19 patients were diagnosed with acquired uterine AVM clinically and through imaging studies. The clinical characteristics, angiographic features, technical success rate of embolization, procedure-related complications, imaging, and clinical follow-up data were assessed. Clinical success was defined as immediate symptomatic resolution with disappearance of vascular abnormality on subsequent imaging studies.
RESULTS: A total of 20 bilateral UAE, with or without embolization of extra-uterine feeders, were performed as the first-line treatment. Technical and clinical success rate was 90.0% (18/20) and 89.5% (17/19), respectively. Embolization was incomplete in two patients who had residual extra-uterine fine feeders to the AVM or a procedure- related complication (ruptured uterine artery); the former showed slow regression of the vascular malformation during the observation period, while the latter underwent a successful second bilateral UAE. Immediate clinical success was achieved in the remaining 17 patients after a single session and no recurrence of bleeding was found. Recovery to normal menstrual cycle was seen in all 17 patients with clinical success within one or two months, two of whom subsequently had uneventful intrauterine pregnancies carried to term.
CONCLUSION: Bilateral UAE is a safe and effective first-line therapeutic option for the management of bleeding uterine AVMs. However, incomplete embolization due to unembolizable feeders or difficult access into the uterine artery may lead to suboptimal treatment.

articles.title: Lasers and laser-like devices: part two.
articles.abstract: Part two of this review series evaluates the use of lasers and laser-like devices in dermatology based on published evidence and the collective experience of the senior authors. Dermatologists can laser-treat a wide range of dermatoses, including vascular, pigmentary, textural, benign proliferative and premalignant conditions. Some of these conditions include vascular malformation, haemangioma, facial telangiectases, café-au-lait macules, naevi of Ota, lentigines, acne scarring, rhytides, rhinophyma and miscellaneous skin lesions. Photodynamic therapy with lasers and intense pulsed light is addressed, with particular reference to actinic keratosis and actinic cheilitis. A treatment algorithm for acne scarring based on scar morphology and severity is comprehensively outlined. Following from part one, the various devices are matched to the corresponding dermatological conditions with representative pictorial case vignettes illustrating likely clinical outcomes as well as limitations and potential complications of the various laser and light therapies.

articles.title: Proteus syndrome review: molecular, clinical, and pathologic features.
articles.abstract: Proteus syndrome is caused by an activating AKT1 mutation (c.49G>A, p.Glu17Lys). Many variable features are possible in this mosaic disorder, including: (i) disproportionate, asymmetric, and distorting overgrowth; (ii) bone abnormalities different from those observed in other disorders; (iii) a characteristic cerebriform connective tissue nevus made up of highly collagenized connective tissue; (iv) epidermal nevi in early life, consisting of acanthosis and hyperkeratosis; (v) vascular malformations of the capillary, venous, or lymphatic types; (vi) dysregulated adipose tissue including lipomas, lipohypoplasia, fatty overgrowth, and localized fat deposits; (vii) other unusual features, including bullous lung alterations; specific neoplasms; a facial phenotype associated with intellectual disability and/or seizures, and/or brain malformations; and (viii) deep vein thrombosis, resulting in premature death. Concluding remarks address diagnostic criteria, natural history, management, psychosocial issues, and differential diagnosis.

articles.title: The double-edged sword: a contemporary perspective on biologics for anti-cytokine syndromes.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Anti-cytokine autoantibodies (ACA) modulate human immunity and may manifest as phenocopies of inborn errors of immunity. Patients typically present with severe, persistent, unusual, or recurrent infections and possible autoimmune manifestations. While prolonged antimicrobials are the traditional standard of care, they frequently lead to drug resistance and adverse effects, highlighting an urgent need for disease-modifying therapies. However, the use of immunosuppressive agents in treating immunodeficiency is a dilemma in the field.
AREAS COVERED: This review synthesizes current clinical evidence on managing ACA syndromes, with specific focus on interferon-γ, granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulating factor, IL-12/23, IL-6, type 1 IFNs, and IL-10. We evaluate the efficacy and therapeutic rationale of various treatments, including B-cell depletion, plasma exchange, and cytokine replacement, while highlighting the distinct clinical phenotypes and diagnostic strategies for each syndrome.
EXPERT OPINION: The use of biologics in ACA marks a shift from reactive antimicrobial treatments to proactive targeted immune reconstitution. Clinical use is still restricted by the inherent risks of immunosuppressing actively infected patients and the absence of standardized functional assays for monitoring. Overcoming these barriers will require accessible ACA screening and the development of customized therapies, such as chimeric autoantibody receptor-T, to deliver functional cures and improve long-term patient care.

articles.title: Hyponatremia in septic shock: Pathophysiology, fluid resuscitation challenges, and neurological complications.
articles.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening condition characterized by organ dysfunction due to a dysregulated host response to infection, with septic shock representing its most severe form and carrying high mortality in intensive care units (ICUs). Among critically ill patients, hyponatremia (serum sodium) <135 mmol/L is a common electrolyte disturbance associated with worse outcomes. While prior studies have explored hypernatremia in septic shock, the pathophysiology, clinical implications, and management of hyponatremia in this context remain underexplored, creating uncertainty for clinicians regarding fluid resuscitation strategies and neurological safety. This narrative review aimed to synthesize current evidence on hyponatremia in septic shock, focusing on underlying mechanisms, resuscitation challenges, and neurological complications. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, EMBASE, and Google Scholar for studies published between 2017 and 2025, including clinical cohorts, case reports, and systematic reviews. The findings indicate that hyponatremia in septic shock arises from non-osmotic vasopressin release, systemic inflammation, acute kidney injury, and fluid shifts during aggressive resuscitation. Large-volume crystalloid administration may exacerbate sodium derangements, while rapid correction poses a risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), even under guideline-adherent practices. Case reports suggest plasma exchange may provide the most consistent benefit in severe neurological complications. In conclusion, hyponatremia in septic shock reflects complex neuroendocrine, inflammatory, and renal interactions. Optimized management requires individualized fluid strategies, cautious sodium correction, and prolonged neurological monitoring to mitigate complications and improve outcomes in critically ill patients.

articles.title: Severe paediatric scrub typhus with complications: a case report and literature review.
articles.abstract: This case report documents a rare case of scrub typhus with multiple serious complications in a 8-year-old patient. Scrub typhus is usually more prevalent in adults, but serious complications in children are uncommon. This report examines a severe pediatric case involving septic shock, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). The patient initially presented with erythema of the umbilicus, which then progressed to characteristic crusting with high fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and enlarged lymph nodes. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) confirmed the presence of Scrub typhus in the patient's blood sample. Notably, this is the first case of scrub typhus found in lung using mNGS, providing strong evidence for early detection. Treatment included a combination of antibiotics, particularly doxycycline and rifampicin, as well as supportive measures such as invasive mechanical ventilation, plasma exchange, continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) and chemotherapy. With this comprehensive treatment approach, the patient's condition gradually improved and he was eventually discharged with complete recovery. This case emphasizes the importance of timely and accurate diagnosis and multidisciplinary supportive care in the treatment of severe scrub typhus in children.

articles.title: Acute kidney injury associated with acute fatty liver of pregnancy: An update on a rare clinical entity.
articles.abstract: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) is a rare but potentially life-threatening liver disease associated with mitochondrial dysfunction. It is characterized by microvesicular hepatic steatosis and typically occurs in the third trimester, though it may rarely present postpartum. AFLP is considered a non-thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) but may present with overlapping TMA features. Its incidence ranges from 1 in 7000 to 1 in 20000 pregnancies, although milder cases may go unrecognized. AFLP can rapidly progress to acute liver failure and 20% to 40% of affected women exhibit clinical features of preeclampsia. Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a frequent complication, observed in 55% to 75% of AFLP cases, which is significantly higher than the 7% to 20% occurrence seen in preeclampsia or hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets syndrome. The exact mechanism behind AKI in AFLP remains unclear, but renal histology has shown tubular deposits of free fatty acids, which correlate with current theories regarding liver pathology. While AFLP-associated AKI is often reversible after delivery, some patients may develop persistent AKI that requires dialysis. Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) has been explored in these cases, but available evidence is limited. This review summarizes the current understanding of the epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical features, and management of AKI in the context of AFLP, and discusses the potential role of adjunctive therapies such as TPE.

articles.title: Multifaceted neuroprotection of ginsenosides: Mechanisms, nano-delivery advances, and therapeutic potential in central nervous system disorders.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Central nervous system (CNS) diseases remain therapeutic challenges due to complex pathology and poor drug penetration across the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Ginsenosides, the active components of Panax ginseng, possess multi-target neuroprotective properties but exhibit low bioavailability.
PURPOSE: This review synthesizes current evidence on ginsenoside mechanisms and evaluates the role of nanotechnology in enhancing their delivery and efficacy for CNS disorders.
STUDY DESIGN: A systematic search was conducted following PRISMA guidelines across PubMed, Web of Science, CNKI, and Google Scholar (2015-present). Included studies investigated ginsenosides in neurological disease models and nano-formulation strategies.
RESULTS: Ginsenosides modulate neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and calcium homeostasis through pathways involving NF-κB, Nrf2, and Bcl-2/Bax. Nano-delivery systems-such as liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, and biomimetic vesicles-significantly improve ginsenoside stability, BBB traversal, and brain-targeted accumulation. Functionalization with ligands (e.g., Angiopep-2) or cell membranes further enhances specificity and therapeutic outcomes in ischemic stroke, glioma, Alzheimer's disease, and spinal cord injury models.
CONCLUSION: Nanotechnology-based delivery systems potently augment the neuroprotective potential of ginsenosides, offering a promising strategy for multi-target CNS therapy. Future efforts should focus on translational safety, scalable production, and clinical validation.

articles.title: Dose-Dependent Autophagic Dysfunction and CCR5-Mediated Neuroinflammation Drive Arsenic Trioxide-Induced Cortical Neurodegeneration in Mice.
articles.abstract: Neurotoxic environmental contaminant arsenic is widely present in global groundwater used for consumption and dietary sources, and has been significantly implicated in cognitive and neurodegenerative diseases. Although of increasing concern, the dose-dependent molecular pathways mediating arsenic-induced corticocerebral neurons dysfunction remain poorly understood, especially regarding the cross-talk between regulation of autophagy and neuroinflammation. This research explored the molecular mechanisms underlying the neurotoxic effects of arsenic trioxide (As2O3) in the mice cerebral cortex, particularly PI3K-AKT-mTOR-regulated autophagic activity and CCR5-induced microglia-driven neuroinflammation, at physiologically and experimentally relevant dosage. Thirty-two adult male Kunming mice were randomly assigned to four groups (n = 8) and orally administered 0, 0.15, 1.5, or 15 ppm As2O3 for 90 days. Quantitative real-time PCR, Western blot, hematoxylin and eosin histomorphometry and transmission electron microscopy were performed on cerebral cortex region. The PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway and autophagy-related genes ATG5, ATG7 and LC3 were significantly increased at low-level exposure reflecting adaptive response, but strongly down-regulated at lethal levels, with concurrent activation of mTOR, revealing defective autophagy. High level treatment led to significant up-regulation of GLS1, CCR5, CCL2, CCL3, CCL5 and Iba1, reflecting glutaminolytic switch and threshold-dependent microglial neuroinflammation. Histological morphometry supported dose-dependent neurodegeneration, with healthy neurons decreasing and the pyknotic index increasing at high doses. Electron microscopy confirmed cytoplasmic vacuole accumulation, mitochondrial cristae distortion, and autophagosomes (AP)-lysosomes (LY) co-accumulation, indicating compromised autophagic flux. These findings reveal that high arsenic exposure may be associated with neurodegeneration involving convergent mTOR-driven autophagic dysfunction, an excitotoxic metabolic shift and CCR5-associated neuroinflammation, pointing to potential mechanistically interlinked therapeutic targets that warrant further functional validation.

articles.title: Mechanistic insights of Artemisia-derived therapeutics in Alzheimer's disease (AD): from crude botanical extracts to artemisinin and derivatives.
articles.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by several pathological processes including amyloid-β (Aβ) accumulation, Tau hyperphosphorylation, oxidative stress, synaptic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial impairment and loss in neuronal stability. This review assessed the reported neuroprotective potential of crude extracts of different Artemisia species and artemisinin with its derivatives in AD. It focuses on targets, mechanisms, observational markers and functional effects validated by Artemisia extracts and compounds like artemisinin, artemisinin B, artemether, artesunate and dihydroartemisinin in experimental AD models. A comprehensive review of studies was conducted including in vitro, in vivo and in silico research on Artemisia extracts and derivatives focusing on their effects on various pathological processes related to brain. Results showed crude extracts from 17 Artemisia species, which have been reported with considerable neuroprotective effects. Artemisinin and derivatives deliver neuroprotection via targeted mechanisms and effecting observational markers with varying functional outcomes. However, differences in AD models, administration routes, doses, extract composition and outcomes limit direct efficacy comparisons. Hence, direct comparisons of efficacy among Artemisia extracts, artemisinin and its derivatives should be interpreted cautiously. Future inquiries should highlight standardized preparations, brain exposure and pharmacokinetics, mechanistic validation, long-term safety and well-designed comparative and clinical trials to evaluate their potential for AD treatment.

articles.title: Persistent Endothelial Glycocalyx Disruption in Sepsis: Translational Evidence for Melatonin-Mediated Vascular Protection.
articles.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome driven by a dysregulated host response to infection, with endothelial dysfunction and glycocalyx disruption playing central roles in vascular failure. Despite growing recognition of the glycocalyx as a therapeutic target, its temporal dynamics and potential pharmacological modulation remain poorly understood. We performed a translational study combining longitudinal clinical observations in septic patients with mechanistic investigations in a murine cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) model. Plasma from patients was collected at intensive care unit admission and after clinical recovery to assess inflammatory mediators, coagulation parameters, and glycocalyx-related biomarkers. In parallel, the CLP model evaluated systemic and tissue-specific glycocalyx alterations and the effects of injectable melatonin. Acute sepsis induced marked alterations in multiple glycocalyx-related biomarkers in patients, with several changes persisting despite normalization of organ dysfunction and standard inflammatory indices, indicating ongoing endothelial injury and repair. In the CLP model, sepsis reproduced these alterations, while melatonin treatment significantly attenuated systemic cytokine responses and partially restored circulating and tissue glycocalyx components in an organ- and gene-specific manner. These results highlight persistent, dynamic glycocalyx disruption as a key driver of sepsis pathology and support pharmacological stabilization of the glycocalyx as a promising therapeutic strategy. Melatonin emerges as a potential endothelial-protective agent capable of promoting vascular recovery and homeostasis, providing translational insight for interventions targeting microvascular integrity in sepsis.

articles.title: Articular Cartilage-Derived Extracellular Matrix Material Promotes a Pro-Regenerative Macrophage Phenotype to Support Chondrogenesis.
articles.abstract: Articular cartilage (AC) repair remains a major clinical challenge due to its limited healing capacity and the inability of current treatment strategies to restore long-term function. Biomaterial-based strategies which support favorable immune responses and appropriate progenitor cell function have shown promise in enhancing cartilage regeneration. We and others have previously demonstrated the capacity of extracellular matrix (ECM)-based materials to direct both innate immune cell behavior and progenitor cell differentiation, with these effects highly dependent on the ECM tissue of origin. Building on these observations, we now aim to further investigate the immunomodulatory properties of AC-derived ECM (AC-ECM) materials. Using primary human macrophages, we demonstrate that AC-ECM material promotes a metabolically active mixed response in macrophages, with elevated expression of reparative growth factors conducive to chondrogenesis. Furthermore, AC-ECM limits inflammatory activation of primary human macrophages, as demonstrated by reduced metabolic reprogramming and inflammatory cytokine production. Functionally, macrophages treated with AC-ECM enhance cartilage regeneration by increasing chondrogenic marker expression in mesenchymal stem cells, while also suppressing angiogenic tube formation in endothelial cells. Overall, this work demonstrates that AC-ECM biomaterials can direct macrophage phenotype toward a pro-chondrogenic state, offering a promising strategy for the development of more effective and durable cartilage repair therapies.

articles.title: [Sepsis-induced coagulopathy].
articles.abstract: Sepsis-induced coagulopathy (SIC) represents a frequent and prognostically highly relevant complication of sepsis, characterized by a dysregulated interaction between inflammation, endothelial activation and coagulation. Pathophysiologically, the excessive host immune response to pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMP) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMP), activation of the complement cascade, formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NET) and disruption of the endothelial glycocalyx collectively promote a prothrombotic and antifibrinolytic microenvironment, resulting in microvascular thrombosis, organ dysfunction and increased mortality. Approximately 20-25% of critically ill patients with sepsis fulfil the diagnostic criteria for SIC. Current diagnostic approaches rely on scoring systems such as the International Society on Thrombosis and Hemostasis (ISTH)-SIC, ISTH overt-disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and Japanese Society on Thrombosis and Hemostasis (JSTH)-DIC scores; however, their clinical utility remains limited as they predominantly collate hemorrhagic parameters even though sepsis is typically characterized by a thrombotically dominated phenotype. Viscoelastic point-of-care assays enable dynamic bedside assessment of coagulation and fibrinolysis, including the frequently occurring hypofibrinolysis or fibrinolytic shutdown, which is associated with an unfavorable outcome; however, for this specific purpose, these methods have not yet been sufficiently validated or established as a diagnostic standard. Data and recommendations on specific therapeutic options are limited. A consistent pharmacological thromboprophylaxis remains the cornerstone in patients with sepsis, with low-molecular weight heparins demonstrating advantages over unfractionated heparin regarding venous thromboembolic complications. Coagulation modulating treatment, such as antithrombin, recombinant thrombomodulin or activated protein C, have thus far failed to demonstrate consistent survival benefits in large randomized clinical trials. Experimental approaches targeting NET formation, complement activation or fibrinolytic modulation appear mechanistically promising but require further clinical validation. Overall, SIC necessitates an individualized, pathophysiology-driven diagnostic and therapeutic approach integrating inflammatory, endothelial, thrombotic and fibrinolytic alterations.

articles.title: Multiple sclerosis occurrence with gut microbial metabolites and sex hormones.
articles.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic immune and neurodegenerative condition that affects the central nervous system (CNS). Multiple factors, both genetic (including the HLA gene locus) and environmental (Epstein-Barr virus, low vitamin D levels), may contribute to MS development. Growing evidence supports the importance of the gut-brain axis and hormones in disease pathogenesis and progression. This review focuses on identifying the role of specific gut microbial products (short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan derivatives, bile acids, and polyamines) in this process and how they affect the immune system, blood-brain barrier (BBB), and glial cells. The review will also describe key differences between female and male patients with MS, including the higher prevalence in females and the tendency toward a progressive course in males. Estrogens, progesterone, and androgens have immunomodulatory, neuroprotective, and remyelinating activities, and this review will describe their impact on multiple sclerosis based on preclinical and clinical findings from pregnancy, menopause, and hormone replacement therapy. This paper discusses the intersection of these ideas through the "microgenderome" concept, which describes how hormones influence gut microbiota composition and how the microbiota, in turn, modulates hormone metabolism and levels.

articles.title: Mechanisms underlying exercise-induced pain modulation in people with multiple sclerosis - a scoping review.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND STUDY AIM: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a prevalent chronic neuroinflammatory disease, characterized by demyelination, inflammation and axonal degeneration. Up to 40% of people with MS (pwMS) experience central neuropathic pain (CNP). Despite numerous debilitating consequences, CNP is often underdiagnosed and undertreated, with limited pharmacological options available. However, exercise is a promising non-pharmacological intervention in the management of pain. This scoping review therefore aims to (a) outline the pathophysiological mechanisms of CNP in MS, (b) summarize the neurophysiological effects of exercise on pain in MS, and (c) identify the mechanistic approaches through which exercise could modulate pain.
METHODS: PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, and SPORTDiscus were searched using terms related to MS, exercise, and pain modulation. We included primary quantitative studies as well as relevant secondary evidence, investigating effects or mechanisms of exercise on recurrent, subacute, or chronic pain in pwMS. In the primary studies, pain was assessed through self-reported or objective measures.
RESULTS: Thirty-six articles were included. Mechanistic findings suggest that neuroinflammation, structural and functional central nervous system changes, and alterations in neurotransmitters and hormones contribute to pain in pwMS. Exercise may modulate several of these mechanisms, including inflammatory markers, neurostructural and functional brain changes, and pathways involving endocannabinoid and tryptophan systems.
CONCLUSION: Exercise may exert beneficial effects on central mechanisms relevant to pain modulation in pwMS, including neuroinflammatory pathways, neuroplastic adaptations, and neurotransmitter regulation. However, existing evidence is limited, warranting further high-quality research to fully clarify mechanistic links and establish exercise as a targeted non-pharmacological treatment for CNP in pwMS.

articles.title: Inhibition of PDGF signal suppresses the fibrotic scar formation and promotes axonal regeneration in a mouse nigrostriatal lesion model.
articles.abstract: After traumatic injury to the central nervous system (CNS), meningeal fibroblasts migrate into the lesion site and synthesize extracellular matrix (ECM) molecules, leading to the formation of a fibrotic scar (FS). The FS prevents axonal regeneration by releasing inhibitory ECMs, including chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, slits, and semaphorin 3 A. Platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) has been implicated in fibrotic diseases, but its specific contribution to FS formation has remained unclear. In this study, we investigated the role of PDGF signaling in scar formation after CNS injury. In the lesioned mouse brain, PDGFRα and PDGFRβ were strongly expressed within the FS, whereas PDGF-B was detected in reactive astrocytes surrounding the lesion. Administration of AG1296, a PDGF signaling inhibitor, into the lesion site significantly reduced FS formation and allowed partial regeneration of transected dopaminergic axons. Complementary in vitro studies using rat meningeal fibroblasts demonstrated that PDGF signaling promoted both proliferation and migration of fibroblasts. Moreover, PDGF stimulation enhanced expression of transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β), a cytokine known to drive ECM deposition and scar formation. These findings provide the first direct evidence that inhibition of PDGF signaling suppresses FS formation and facilitates axonal regeneration after CNS lesioning. Our results suggest that PDGF signaling functions during the early phase of FS development by promoting fibroblast proliferation, migration, and TGF-β expression. Thus, targeting PDGF signaling may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for limiting scar formation and improving neural repair following human CNS injury.NEW & NOTEWORTHY Our research has revealed that PDGF signaling, which is known to be involved in various fibrotic diseases, also contributes to fibrotic scar formation-a barrier to nerve regeneration in the lesioned brain. This signaling plays a role in both the initiation and maintenance of fibrotic scar formation. Indeed, inhibiting PDGF signaling in vivo resulted in the disappearance of the fibrotic scar, thereby enabling nerve regeneration.

articles.title: Mechanical immune checkpoints in tumors: Mechanosensing, immunosuppressive networks, and therapeutic modulation.
articles.abstract: Solid tumors undergo significant biomechanical remodeling, which includes ECM stiffening, collagen crosslinking and alignment, increased interstitial fluid pressure, solid stress, vascular compression, and altered viscoelastic properties. These biomechanical abnormalities function not merely as passive structural features but actively influence tumor progression and immune evasion. Emerging evidence introduces the concept of mechanical immune checkpoints, defined as mechanosensory immunoregulatory circuits that link specific biomechanical signals to impaired antitumor immunity through identifiable mechanosensory or mechanotransduction pathways This review first summarizes the mechanisms through which aberrant tumor mechanics contribute to T-cell exclusion, T-cell exhaustion, suppressive myeloid differentiation, and stromal remodeling. Subsequently, it discusses therapeutic strategies, including ECM remodeling, inhibition of mechanotransduction, modulation of mechanosensors and tumor cell stiffness, as well as rational combinations with traditional immune checkpoint blockade. Lastly, the translational maturity of current strategies is critically assessed, highlighting priorities for biomarker-guided combination therapy. By conceptualizing force-sensitive immunosuppressive circuits within a clinically relevant framework, mechanical immune checkpoints may facilitate biomarker-guided patient stratification and rational combination approaches to enhance immunotherapy efficacy in mechanically resistant solid tumors.
